120.title: The bedtime Shema
120.hook: before sleep: the Shema, and forgiveness for anyone who hurt you that day
120.howItsDone: Before sleep, many Jews say the bedtime Shema: a declaration forgiving anyone who wronged them, the Shema, the Hamapil blessing, and verses such as Psalm 31:6 and the line about the four angels.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Baruch Dayan HaEmet, three words inside grief, and then silence. Your line was even here, a word. Today, the last blessing of the day, and the last day of this part of the path. Day one hundred twenty.

It's late. The lights are off. You're in bed, and your body is tired, but your mind is wide awake, replaying the day. What she said in the meeting. The text he never answered. The driver who cut you off. You write your comeback in your head, again. It's midnight, then one. Plenty of us fall asleep, when we finally do, holding a grudge like a pillow. Jewish tradition has a practice for exactly this hour, and its first step isn't a prayer. It's letting go. Today: the bedtime Shema.
screen: `THE LIGHTS ARE OFF.` → `REPLAYING THE DAY.` → `ASLEEP, HOLDING A GRUDGE.`

segments.voice: Way back in camp one, you learned the Shema, the line at the heart of Jewish prayer. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." And the Torah says to speak these words "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." So Jews say the Shema in the evening prayers. But the Talmud says to say it again, in bed, right before sleep. It points to a line from the Psalms: "commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still." Over the centuries, the bedtime Shema grew into a short bedtime service. Many prayer books begin it with something remarkable. Before the Shema, before anything, a person says that they forgive anyone who angered or hurt them that day, in body, money, honor or anything else, whether by accident or on purpose, and asks that no one be punished on their account. The Talmud tells of a rabbi, Mar Zutra, who did this every night: before going to bed, he said, I forgive everyone who troubled me. Then comes the Shema, and a blessing thanking God, who lets sleep fall on my eyes. Many say a line from a psalm: "Into Thy hand I commit my spirit." And in many homes, children and adults say a line about four angels: Michael on my right, Gabriel on my left, Uriel in front, Raphael behind, and above my head, God's presence. Remember the two angels who walked you home on Friday night? They come back at bedtime. So look at the shape of the day you've learned in this part of the path. It opens with thank you, Modeh Ani, before your feet touch the floor. It closes with I forgive you, before your eyes close. Blessings all the way through.
screen: `THE SHEMA, AGAIN, IN BED.` · `I FORGIVE ANYONE WHO HURT ME.` · `MAR ZUTRA, EVERY NIGHT.` · `FOUR ANGELS AROUND THE BED.` · then, large: `INTO THY HAND I COMMIT MY SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive one thing before you sleep. Let's practice it now, so it's ready tonight. Settle, and breathe. Let one small hurt from today, or this week, come to mind. Not the biggest one. Something you can manage. Picture the person. You don't have to say they were right. You don't have to call them. Just set it down, the way you'd put a heavy bag on the floor before bed. Say to yourself: I forgive this, for tonight. If you pray, you can hand it to God. The bell holds the time.
The bedtime Shema. The last prayer of the day, said in bed: forgiveness first, then the Shema, and sleep in God's hand.
Your line: forgive before sleeping. Tonight, in bed, let one thing go before you close your eyes. Tomorrow a new part begins: the holidays, starting with the calendar. Day one hundred twenty.

121.title: The Jewish calendar
121.hook: a lunar year with a leap month seven times in nineteen years, so festivals keep their seasons
121.howItsDone: Jewish communities keep a lunisolar calendar: months follow the moon, a second Adar is added seven times in nineteen years, and each day, Shabbat and festival begins at sunset. Many families keep a printed luach from their synagogue.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bedtime Shema: the last words of the day, and a quiet line forgiving anyone who hurt you. Your line was forgive before sleeping. Did you let one thing go last night? Day one hundred twenty-one.

Ask a Jewish friend when Hanukkah is this year, and there's a good chance they'll have to look it up. Last year it was early December. Another year it lands right on top of Christmas. Passover drifts around March and April. Rosh Hashanah can come in early September or in October. It looks like the holidays wander. They don't. They're keeping perfect time, just not on the clock on your phone. For the next few weeks we walk through the Jewish year, one holiday at a time, as they arrive. And before any holiday, you need the thing that holds them all.
screen: `WHEN IS HANUKKAH THIS YEAR?` → `THE HOLIDAYS SEEM TO WANDER.` → `THEY'RE KEEPING A DIFFERENT CLOCK.`

segments.voice: The Hebrew word for a calendar is luach. It means a tablet or a board, the same word used for the tablets Moses carried down the mountain. Today a luach is often a printed calendar on a synagogue wall, or an app. The Jewish calendar runs on the moon. Each month begins at the new moon and lasts twenty-nine or thirty days, because that's how long the moon takes to go from dark to dark. In the first chapter of Genesis, the lights in the sky are made "for signs, and for seasons, and for days and years." And the Psalms say it plainly: "Who appointedst the moon for seasons." Here's the problem. Twelve moon months add up to about three hundred fifty-four days. The sun's year is about eleven days longer. A purely lunar calendar slides backward through the seasons, and the Torah ties Passover to spring and Sukkot to the harvest. So the Jewish calendar does something clever: seven times in every nineteen years, it adds a whole extra month, a second Adar, in late winter. That leap month pulls the moon back in line with the sun, and Passover stays in spring. For centuries, a new month was declared by a court in Jerusalem when witnesses reported seeing the thin new moon. Later, tradition says in the fourth century, the calendar was fixed by calculation, so Jews scattered around the world could keep the same days. Two more things. A Jewish day begins at sunset, because Genesis says "there was evening and there was morning." And the years are counted from creation, as the rabbis reckoned it, so the year that began this September is five thousand seven hundred eighty-seven.
screen: `LUACH: A TABLET, A CALENDAR.` · `EACH MONTH BEGINS AT THE NEW MOON.` · `A LEAP MONTH, SEVEN TIMES IN NINETEEN.` · `THE DAY BEGINS AT SUNSET.` · then, large: `THE MOON FOR SEASONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find today's Hebrew date. Afterward, look it up on any Jewish calendar or online. For now, settle, and breathe. Notice the time of day you're in. If it's evening, remember that on this calendar, tomorrow has already begun. Think of one date that matters to you, a birthday, an anniversary, the day someone died. Wonder what it was on the moon's calendar. Just hold the idea that there's more than one way to count a life. The bell holds the time.
Luach. A tablet, and the Jewish calendar: moon months, kept in step with the sun by a leap month seven times in nineteen years.
Your line: the moon keeps time. Tonight, notice where the day ends: watch the sun go down and say, quietly, a new day starts now. Day one hundred twenty-one.

122.title: The new moon
122.hook: each new month is a small holiday, long honored especially by women
122.howItsDone: On Rosh Chodesh, synagogues add a short Hallel, a Torah reading and an additional service. Many women mark the day with study groups or by setting aside some work, and some communities bless the growing moon a few days later.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the luach: a calendar of moon months, with a leap month to keep the seasons. Your line was the moon keeps time. Did you catch the sunset, the moment a new day began? Day one hundred twenty-two.

Picture a hilltop near Jerusalem, two thousand years ago, just after sunset. Two people are squinting at the western sky, looking for the thinnest sliver of moon, barely there. They see it. They hurry to the court in Jerusalem and testify. The judges question them: where was it, which way did it point? When the testimony holds, the court declares it: the new month has begun. The Mishnah says that news once traveled by torches waved from mountaintop to mountaintop, all the way to the Jews in Babylon. All that, for the first day of a month.
screen: `A SLIVER OF MOON AT SUNSET.` → `WITNESSES RUN TO THE COURT.` → `TORCHES FROM HILL TO HILL.`

segments.voice: The first day of every Jewish month has a name: Rosh Chodesh. Rosh means head, and chodesh means month, from a root that means new. So a month, in Hebrew, is literally a newness. Every month starts with a small holiday. It isn't a day off work. But in the synagogue there's an extra prayer service, the psalms of praise called Hallel are sung in a shorter form, and a special Torah reading is added. In the Torah itself, the new moons stand beside the festivals: the Book of Numbers speaks of blowing trumpets "in the day of your gladness, and in your appointed seasons, and in your new moons." In the Bible's stories, it's a day for a family meal; King Saul notices that David's seat is empty at the new moon feast. And here is the part many people never hear. Rosh Chodesh has long been honored as a special day for women. An old midrash tells that when the people built the golden calf, the women refused to hand over their gold jewelry for it, and so they were given the new moons as a holiday of their own. For centuries, in many communities, women kept the day by not doing certain heavy work. In recent decades, many Jewish women have gathered in Rosh Chodesh groups, to study, sing and talk, month by month. There's one more custom: a few days after the new moon, when the moon is growing, some Jews go outside at night and say a blessing over it. Why does the moon matter so much? Because it shrinks, disappears, and comes back. The rabbis saw in it a picture of the Jewish people, and of anyone who has ever had to start again.
screen: `ROSH CHODESH: HEAD OF THE MONTH.` · `A SMALL HOLIDAY EVERY MONTH.` · `A DAY FOR WOMEN.` · `THE MOON SHRINKS AND COMES BACK.` · then, large: `AND IN YOUR NEW MOONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for the moon tonight. Before that, settle, and breathe. Think about where the moon is right now, even if you can't see it: growing, full, shrinking, or gone dark. Then think of one part of your life that feels like the dark of the moon, something that's gone quiet. You don't have to fix it. Just remember that dark is part of the cycle, not the end of it. The bell holds the time.
Rosh Chodesh. The head of the month: the new moon, kept as a small holiday, and long honored as a day for women.
Your line: renew with the moon. Tonight, step outside and find the moon, or the place where it would be, and let one thing start over. Day one hundred twenty-two.

123.title: Rosh Hashanah: the shofar
123.hook: the new year opens with a ram's horn, a cry without words
123.howItsDone: On Rosh Hashanah, a shofar is sounded in the synagogue in patterns of tekiah, shevarim and teruah, traditionally a hundred blasts over the day, except on Shabbat. Many communities also blow it each weekday morning in the month of Elul beforehand.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rosh Chodesh, the head of the month, a small holiday at every new moon. Your line was renew with the moon. Did you find it in the sky? Day one hundred twenty-three.

Most new years begin with a countdown and a lot of noise. The Jewish new year begins with noise too, but of a very different kind. A synagogue, full. Someone stands with a curved animal horn, lifts it to their lips, and the room goes silent. Then it comes: one long, raw, rising note. Then three broken ones, like sighing. Then nine short, fast blasts, like sobbing. People who have heard it all their lives still say it goes straight through them. No words at all. That is how Rosh Hashanah, the head of the year, opens.
screen: `A NEW YEAR WITHOUT A COUNTDOWN.` → `A CURVED HORN, A SILENT ROOM.` → `A CRY WITH NO WORDS.`

segments.voice: The horn is called a shofar. It's usually a ram's horn, hollowed out, and it's not really an instrument; it has no keys and plays no tune. The Torah never uses the name Rosh Hashanah for this day. It calls the first day of the seventh month "a day of blowing the horn unto you." That's the whole description: a day of the horn. The rabbis later named it the head of the year, and taught that on this day the whole world is judged. There are three sounds. Tekiah, one long blast. Shevarim, three broken notes. Teruah, many short staccato ones. The rabbis weren't sure exactly what the Torah's teruah sounded like, a groan or a whimper, so they kept both, and the old custom is to hear the sounds in many combinations, adding up to a hundred blasts over the day. The last one is the tekiah gedolah, the great blast, held as long as the blower's breath will last. Why a ram's horn? Because it calls to mind the ram that Abraham offered in place of Isaac. A cow's horn isn't used; the rabbis said it would recall the golden calf. And what does it mean? The great philosopher Maimonides, eight hundred years ago, said the shofar carries a message even though the Torah gives no reason: wake up, you sleepers, from your sleep. Look at your deeds. Come back. Others hear a coronation trumpet, or a child crying out to a parent without words. Jewish tradition holds all of these. On the Sabbath it isn't blown, and in many communities it's sounded every weekday morning in the month before, like an alarm set early.
screen: `A DAY OF BLOWING THE HORN.` · `TEKIAH, SHEVARIM, TERUAH.` · `A RAM, NOT A COW.` · `WAKE UP, YOU SLEEPERS.` · then, large: `A CRY WITHOUT WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to a shofar once. Later, find a recording and let it play all the way through. For now, settle, and breathe. Take one long breath in and let it out slowly, like a tekiah. Then three broken breaths out, like shevarim. Then breathe normally, and ask one question: what have I been asleep to? A person, a habit, a feeling. Don't answer out loud. Just let the question sound. The bell holds the time.
Shofar. A ram's horn, blown on Rosh Hashanah in long, broken and short blasts: a cry without words that says wake up.
Your line: wake up. Today, when a phone buzzes or an alarm goes off, let it be your shofar: stop for one breath and look at what you're doing. Day one hundred twenty-three.

124.title: Rosh Hashanah: apples, honey, water
124.hook: sweet food for a sweet year, and crumbs cast into flowing water
124.howItsDone: On Rosh Hashanah eve, many Jewish families eat apples dipped in honey and a round challah, often with other symbolic foods. On the first afternoon, many go to flowing water for tashlich, reading verses from Micah and sometimes tossing crumbs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shofar: a ram's horn, a cry with no words. Your line was wake up. Did something buzz and stop you for a breath? Day one hundred twenty-four.

The shofar is serious. The table that night is sweet. On the eve of Rosh Hashanah, families sit down to a round challah, the braided bread shaped into a circle for a year that comes around again. Someone passes a plate of apple slices and a small bowl of honey. You dip, and before you eat, you say a line many Jews have said for centuries: may it be God's will that this be a good and sweet year. Then the next afternoon, you might see something stranger: whole families standing on a riverbank, turning out their pockets.
screen: `A ROUND CHALLAH.` → `APPLES DIPPED IN HONEY.` → `FAMILIES ON A RIVERBANK.`

segments.voice: Start with the table. The Talmud mentions foods eaten at the new year as good signs, things that grow quickly or come in abundance. Over time, communities built whole menus around wordplay. Pomegranates, for merits as many as their seeds. In some homes, the head of a fish, so we'll be the head and not the tail. Dates, carrots, leeks and beets, because their Hebrew or Yiddish names sound like wishes. Apples and honey are simply the best known: sweetness, said out loud. Then comes the water. On the first afternoon of Rosh Hashanah, many Jews walk to a river, a stream, a lake or the sea, anywhere the water moves and, ideally, fish live. They read verses from the prophet Micah, which end with a picture of God's mercy: "And Thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea." The ceremony is named for that word, cast: tashlich, you will cast. Many people bring bread crumbs and toss them in, one crumb for each thing they want to leave behind. Here's what's honest to say about it. Tashlich isn't in the Torah or the Talmud. It shows up in Germany in the late Middle Ages, and some rabbis were uneasy with it, worried people would think crumbs in a river could wash away sins by themselves. Jewish teaching is clear that they can't. The work of changing belongs to the ten days that follow, the Days of Awe, leading to Yom Kippur. Tashlich is a picture of that work, not a substitute for it. But what a picture. You stand at moving water, and you let something go.
screen: `FOODS THAT SOUND LIKE WISHES.` · `APPLES AND HONEY: A SWEET YEAR.` · `CAST INTO THE DEPTHS OF THE SEA.` · `A PICTURE, NOT A SHORTCUT.` · then, large: `TASHLICH: YOU WILL CAST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: toss a crumb or a pebble into water. It could be a river, a fountain, even a sink with the tap running. For now, settle, and breathe. Name, silently, one thing you'd like to leave behind this year. A habit. A grudge. A way you talked to someone. Picture holding it in your hand like a crumb. Picture the water. Then, when you get the chance, let it go in and watch it move away. The bell holds the time.
Tashlich. You will cast: a custom of standing by moving water on Rosh Hashanah, reading Micah, and letting go.
Your line: throw it in the river. Today, eat one sweet thing slowly, and let one small resentment go with it. Day one hundred twenty-four.

125.title: Yom Kippur: the fast
125.hook: twenty-five hours without food, drink or leather shoes, like angels for a day
125.howItsDone: On Yom Kippur, many Jews fast for about twenty-five hours, avoid leather shoes and washing, wear white, and spend much of the day in synagogue prayer. Those whose health is at risk are required to eat, and children do not fast.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tashlich: standing at moving water and letting something go. Your line was throw it in the river. What did you let float away? Ten days after Rosh Hashanah comes the holiest day of the year. Day one hundred twenty-five.

Think about how many times a day you reach for something. A coffee. A snack. Water. Your phone. A mirror. Most of it is automatic; you don't even notice. Now imagine a day when you put all of that down. No food. Not even water. No leather shoes. No lotion, no washing up. From just before sunset to after nightfall the next day, about twenty-five hours. Many Jews wear white, and spend most of the day in the synagogue, standing, praying, remembering. And a strange thing happens: people say the hunger fades into something lighter.
screen: `HOW OFTEN DO YOU REACH FOR SOMETHING?` → `PUT IT ALL DOWN.` → `TWENTY-FIVE HOURS.`

segments.voice: Yom Kippur means the Day of Atonement. The word kippur comes from a root often understood as covering, or wiping clean. The Torah says: "For on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins shall ye be clean before the LORD." And it gives one instruction for the body: "ye shall afflict your souls." The rabbis read that as five things to go without: eating and drinking, washing, anointing with oils, wearing leather shoes, and marital intimacy. Why leather? Leather shoes were the comfortable, fine shoes; on this day you walk a little closer to the ground. And why white? There's an old idea that on Yom Kippur Jews are like angels: angels don't eat or drink, they stand, and they wear white. So for one day, people set aside the body's needs and stand like them. Two things matter as much as the fast. First, the fast is never allowed to endanger a life. Anyone who is ill, pregnant with complications, or at risk is told to eat, and Jewish law calls eating in that case a duty, not a failure. Children don't fast. Second, Yom Kippur has a limit that surprises people. The Mishnah teaches that this day atones for wrongs between a person and God. For wrongs between one person and another, it doesn't, until you've gone to the person you hurt and tried to make it right. So in the days before, many Jews call, text or knock on doors and ask: if I hurt you this year, forgive me. The hungry day in the synagogue comes after the harder conversation.
screen: `YOM KIPPUR: THE DAY OF ATONEMENT.` · `FIVE THINGS SET ASIDE.` · `LIKE ANGELS FOR A DAY.` · `FIRST, GO TO THE PERSON YOU HURT.` · then, large: `FROM ALL YOUR SINS SHALL YE BE CLEAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: skip one comfort today. Not your meals, not your medicine, nothing that matters for your health. Something small: the second coffee, the scroll before bed, the snack you don't need. For now, settle, and breathe. Notice what it feels like to not reach for something. Then think of one person you may have hurt this year. Just hold their name. You don't have to call yet. The bell holds the time.
Yom Kippur. The Day of Atonement: twenty-five hours of fasting and prayer, after first making peace with the people you've hurt.
Your line: lighter for a day. Today, set down one small comfort, and notice what you reach for instead. Day one hundred twenty-five.

126.title: Yom Kippur: the gates close
126.hook: the day opens with Kol Nidre and ends as the gates of prayer close
126.howItsDone: Yom Kippur begins with Kol Nidre, chanted three times at sunset, and ends with Neilah, prayed standing before the open ark. It closes with the Shema, 'The LORD, He is God' seven times, and a long blast of the shofar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yom Kippur: twenty-five hours of fasting, standing like angels, after first making peace with the people you hurt. Your line was lighter for a day. What comfort did you set down? Day one hundred twenty-six.

Yom Kippur has a beginning and an end that people remember for the rest of their lives. It begins at sunset. The synagogue is packed. The Torah scrolls are taken out and held. And a cantor sings a haunting old melody, three times, each time a little louder: Kol Nidre. Then, a whole day later, as the light starts to fade and everyone is hungry, tired, and still standing, the last prayer of the day begins. The doors of the ark stay open. People who sat through the afternoon get to their feet. They know what time it is.
screen: `SUNSET: KOL NIDRE, THREE TIMES.` → `A WHOLE DAY OF PRAYER.` → `THE LIGHT STARTS TO FADE.`

segments.voice: First, the opening. Kol Nidre means all vows. It isn't really a prayer; it's a legal formula, in Aramaic, releasing the vows a person makes to God and can't keep. Jewish law is clear that it doesn't cancel promises made to other people; those have to be kept or made right with the person. What gives it its power is the melody and the moment: a whole community admitting that we promise more than we manage. Now the end. The final service of Yom Kippur is called Neilah. The word means locking, or closing. The rabbis remembered that in the Temple, a closing prayer was said as the great gates were locked at sunset. And they also spoke of the gates of heaven, open all day to prayer, now swinging shut. So Neilah feels like the last minutes before a door closes. All through these days, the prayers have asked God to write us in the book of life. In Neilah, the word changes: seal us. The writing is almost done. Then the ending comes all at once. The whole congregation says the Shema, once. Then, three times, the line that follows it, blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom for ever and ever. Then, seven times, the words Elijah's people shouted on Mount Carmel: "The LORD, He is God." And one long blast of the shofar. The fast is over. Many say next year in Jerusalem, and go home to eat. What a week this has been: the bedtime Shema, the calendar, the new moon, the shofar, the river, the fast, and now the gates.
screen: `KOL NIDRE: ALL VOWS.` · `NEILAH: THE GATES ARE CLOSING.` · `WRITE US, THEN SEAL US.` · `THE SHEMA, AND ONE LONG BLAST.` · then, large: `THE LORD, HE IS GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: end today with one quiet sentence. For now, rehearse it. Settle, and breathe. Imagine the day is almost over and the gates are closing. What's the one thing you'd still want to say? To God, if you pray. To someone you love. To yourself. Keep it to one sentence. Let it get simpler with each breath, until it's only a few words. Tonight, before you sleep, say it. The bell holds the time.
Neilah. The closing: the last prayer of Yom Kippur, said as the gates close, ending with the Shema and one long blast.
Your line: before the gates close. Today, don't leave the important sentence for tomorrow; say it while the day is still open. Day one hundred twenty-six.
